newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Battered Albania aims to fix judicial system.
newsitem.headline: Battered Albania aims to fix judicial system.

text.p: Albania boosted security for judges on Tuesday and worked to repair ransacked jails as the government struggled to restore law and order.

Special police forces were assigned to guard magistrates in Tirana and an armoured personel carrier (APC) took up position in front of the Tirana district court, a symbolic gesture as the court -- closed for weeks in the wake of violence -- prepared to reopen within days.
More than 200 people have been killed and 700 injured in weeks of armed rampage in Europe's poorest state, sparked by the collapse of shady savings schemes.
"If police arrest suspected criminals, we need a place to put them," an Interior Ministry official told Reuters.
"It is up to the court to decide if the suspects are guilty or not," he added. "That is why it is important that the courts reopen as soon as possible."
Albania is waiting for an Italian-led multinational force of up to 6,000 troops which will protect the delivery of emergency supplies and which is due to start arriving on April 14.

In Italy, deputy foreign minister Piero Fassino said Albanian President Sali Berisha should leave office but that Rome will not push for his resignation now. It was the first open indication that Italy has withdrawn support from the embattled rightist.

Although the violence has subsided lately as a night curfew has taken hold, police in the port city of Durres 40 km (25 miles) west of Tirana said on Tuesday that three people were killed during the night.
Two mechanics were shot dead after four gunmen drove into a garage, police said. They captured the killers but knew of no motive for the attack.
In a separate incident in Durres, Albania's second largest city with 100,000 residents, a man was shot dead trying to steal a car.
A police spokesman said 2,500 weapons, including 100 machine guns, have been confiscated from local residents in recent weeks.

More than 1,300 prisoners held in the nation's seven dilapidated jails escaped or left during the early days of the mayhem that began in early March, with some fleeing convicts destroying and burning wings of the buildings on their way out.

Fewer than 20 prisoners have returned to two jails still operating, but authorities are optimistic many of the 1,309 who left will take advantage of an amnesty programme that cuts jail terms by one-third to those who voluntarily surrender by April 12. About 600 will not have to return because of the amnesty.

"We hope that by midnight on April 11th a lot will be back," Bedri Coku, the director of Albanian prison system, told Reuters. "Even though the Tirana jail has been seriously damaged in the unrest, we are working to repair it and believe we can have it in shape for 400 people by April 11."
But Coku said jails in areas, particularly in the south, controlled by rebels will not be reopened soon.
"We cannot afford to send convicts to areas where the government is still facing problems," Coku said.
Last month one jail in Tepelene in the south was burned to the ground by the fleeing prisoners, many of whom are thought to have escaped abroad.
The rebuilt justice and prison systems were the latest signs that life was slowly returning to normal in at least parts of Albania.
The country's military academy in Tirana reopened on Friday, the first school of any type to reopen after the insurrection.

On Monday, Albania's soccer federation said it hopes to resume national league play next month in a few towns under police control. Soccer is the nation's most popular sport, passionately followed by Albania's 3.4 million population.
